title: What is Java?
content: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995. Today it powers Android apps, banking systems, Netflix, Amazon, and Spring Boot backends.
The three core pieces are JDK (Java Development Kit), JRE (Java Runtime Environment), and JVM (Java Virtual Machine).

title: Hello, World!
tagline: Your very first Java program, dissected
content: Every Java program lives inside a class.
The main method is the JVM entry point: public static void main(String[] args).

title: Variables and Data Types
tagline: Java's typed boxes for storing data
content: Java has 8 primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean.
Reference types live on the heap: String, arrays, and the objects you create.

title: Operators
content: Java supports arithmetic, comparison, assignment, and logical operators.
Be careful with integer division: 7 / 2 equals 3. Use 7.0 / 2 for decimal division.

title: Strings
content: Strings in Java are immutable, which means methods like toUpperCase() return a new String.
Use StringBuilder when you need efficient concatenation inside loops.

title: If, Else, and Switch
content: if/else chains and switch statements control program flow.
Modern switch expressions reduce fall-through bugs and make code easier to read.

title: Loops
content: Loops let you repeat work safely and clearly.
Use for-each when you do not need the index, and watch for infinite loops.

title: Arrays and Methods
content: Arrays are fixed-size sequences.
Methods help you structure behavior, reuse logic, and visualize the call stack.

title: Classes and Objects
content: A class defines fields and methods. Objects are instances of a class.
Use private fields and public methods to encapsulate state.

title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
content: Inheritance lets a subclass extend a superclass.
Polymorphism lets you treat different subclasses through a shared parent type.

title: Interfaces and Abstract Classes
tagline: Design contracts, not just inheritance trees
content: Interfaces define a contract that classes can implement.
Abstract classes let you share code while still forcing subclasses to provide missing details.

title: Collections Intro
content: Learn ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, and HashSet, and understand when to use each one.
The Collections framework gives you a shared set of interfaces and implementations.

title: Generics
content: Generics let you write classes and methods that work with a type parameter.
They prevent unsafe casts and help the compiler catch mistakes earlier.

title: Exceptions
content: Use try, catch, and finally to handle exceptions.
Throw custom exceptions when a domain rule is broken.

title: File I/O
content: Use Files, Path, BufferedReader, and BufferedWriter for modern file handling.
Prefer try-with-resources so streams close automatically.

title: Streams and Lambdas
content: Streams let you map, filter, and reduce collections in a declarative style.
Lambdas let you pass behavior into methods in a compact form.

title: Concurrency and Threads
content: Use Thread, Runnable, and the java.util.concurrent package for concurrency.
Prefer Executors, avoid shared mutable state, and coordinate access carefully.

title: JVM Internals
tagline: Source code to bytecode to machine code
content: The compiler turns .java files into bytecode, which the JVM loads, verifies, and executes.
The JVM can interpret bytecode at first, then use JIT compilation to speed up hot paths.

title: Build Tools: Maven and Gradle
content: Maven and Gradle automate compilation, testing, and dependency management.
Learn the project structure, the lifecycle, and the commands you will use every day.
